posts.title: Salesforce Admin Foundations
posts.lexical:
{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

Start where every Salesforce career starts

Before automation, before Apex, there is the data model. This course walks through the objects, fields and relationships that hold a Salesforce org together, then layers on the sharing model that decides who sees what. Nothing here assumes prior experience.

What you'll be able to do

  • Read an org's schema and explain how its objects relate
  • Create users, profiles and permission sets without guesswork
  • Choose the right automation tool for a given requirement
"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}

{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

Code that survives contact with production

Apex is easy to write and easy to write badly. This course is about the difference. Every pattern here is framed by the limits the platform imposes, because those limits are what separate code that works on your laptop from code that works on a data load of fifty thousand records.

Prerequisites

You should be comfortable with the standard data model \u2014 take Admin Foundations first if objects and relationships are still fuzzy.

"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}

posts.title: Introduction
posts.lexical:
{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

This site is built on a small design system called Developer Console. Five rules carry it: the hairline border is the structure, monospace is the label material, one signal blue means interactive, geometry is sharp and specific, and motion is instant.

How the CSS is organised

Four layers \u2014 0-foundation (tokens), 1-elements (bare HTML), 2-components (the UI library) and 3-modules (features). Each layer has an index.css listing its files.

"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}

posts.title: Components
posts.lexical:
{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

Every component follows one contract: .ns-thing is the base, .ns-thing--variant changes one axis (size, shape, tone or state), .ns-thing__part names an internal part, and .is-state is toggled by a script.

Variants compose

A large interactive card with a grid pattern is .ns-card .ns-card--lg .ns-card--interactive .ns-card--grid \u2014 no new class required.

"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}

posts.title: Why I reach for Flow before Apex
posts.lexical:
{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

The least powerful tool that works

There's a habit among developers moving into the Salesforce ecosystem: reach for code, because code is what we know. It's the wrong instinct here more often than it's right.

What Flow buys you

Every admin on the team can read it, it upgrades with the platform, and it doesn't need a test class. That's not a small list.

When Apex genuinely wins

Complex bulk logic, callouts with real error handling, and anything you need to unit test properly. Those are real reasons. \"I'm faster in code\" is not.

"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Apex is not the senior choice. Choosing the least powerful tool that solves the problem is.

posts.title: A mental model for governor limits
posts.lexical:
{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

They're not arbitrary

Governor limits look like a list of trivia until you see what they're for: you are a tenant in a shared building, and the limits are the rules that stop one tenant flooding everyone else's flat.

The one rule that covers most of them

Do work in sets, not one record at a time. No SOQL in a loop, no DML in a loop. Almost every limit you'll hit in practice is a variation of breaking that.

"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Stop memorising the numbers. Understand what the platform is protecting and the numbers follow.

posts.title: Your first 90 days as a Salesforce admin
posts.lexical:
{"root": {"children": [{"type": "html", "version": 1, "html": "

Read before you write

The instinct on day one is to fix things. Resist it for a fortnight. An org you didn't build is full of decisions whose reasons aren't written down.

Weeks 1\u20132: map it

Schema Builder, the field usage, and the reports people actually run. Ask who uses what.

Weeks 3\u20136: fix the cheap things

Broken validation messages, unused fields, dashboards nobody opens. Build trust with small wins.

Weeks 7\u201312: change something that matters

By now you've earned the right to have an opinion about the sales process.

"}], "direction": null, "format": "", "indent": 0, "type": "root", "version": 1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: What to actually do when you inherit an org you didn't build.

Salesforce learning material is either a sales pitch or a wall of reference docs. This site is the thing in between: practical, project-led lessons written by people who use the platform every day.

What's here

  • Blog \u2014 opinions, patterns and field notes
